## Q4 Much Weaker Than Initial Data Suggested 



- As more data comes in it is now clear that Q4 2008 was much weaker than we had first estimated. We now believe that for the whole of 2008 global copper wirerod consumption fell by 1.6% to 13.6 million tonnes conductor, with the 3.1 million tonnes of copper consumed in Q4 being the lowest volume since Q4 2004. 



- There was no growth in Eastern Europe, and as a result total European copper wire and cable production fell by 3.1%. The market in North America has continued to deteriorate and has ended the year with a double digit decline. The North East Asian market has also continued to fall, and latest data shows that the ASEAN region also saw a fall in copper cable production. The Rest of the World was sustained by further growth in the GCC countries of the Middle East, but this market is now running out of steam. 



- With such a weak end to the year the outlook for 2009 is looking increasingly poor. Around the world markets are continuing to fall, so comparisons with a strong Q1 2008 will look very bad. If consumption can match Q4 this will still mean a year-on-year fall of over 12%, and it looks certain that H1 2009 will be down more than 10% and maybe 15%. With the fall in copper prices market values could be down by 40% or more this year.

© 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 3 of 12 March 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # Europe ### **European demand tumbles in Q4, weakness continues in 2009** Our latest figures confirm that European wirerod consumption and production slumped in Q4 2008, falling 5.6% and 9% y-o-y respectively. Western Europe fared worst, with consumption and production down 11.7% and 15.2% respectively. Wire and cable demand was down 3.9%, whilst output was down 5.2%. Indications are that this weakness has continued, and in some instances, worsened, in 2009. We expect that Q1 2009 figures will be down further year-on-year. The demand downturn has not been equally felt in all sectors, however. Power cables remain relatively strong, whilst the automotive and construction sectors continue to weaken. Thus far there are few indications that stimulus and infrastructure packages are having a marked impact on the market. In Q4 2008, combined wirerod output by Norddeutsche Affinerie/Cumerio (soon to become Aurubis) amounted to 159,000t, down from a combined total of 227,700t in Q4 2007 (NA: 107,000t, Cumerio: 120,700t). The company responded to the lower utilisation of their plants by extending their Christmas standstill, and reducing the number of temporary employees in an effort to reduce costs. Demand from their largest volume segment, energy cable for conversion and distribution of electricity, remained reasonably steady, with only a slight fall. However, other end use segments fared less well. Some enamelled wire producers, particularly in Southern Europe, saw their business falling by as much as 30%. Wirerod demand from the automotive market also declined, with orders falling by as much as 50%. Nexans reported that its energy infrastructure business held up strongly in 2008, with full-year sales growth of 19.5%. High-voltage cables performed particularly strongly. Booked orders are sufficient to take Nexans into 2010. Medium and low voltage cables also enjoyed significant growth of 10.8%, despite a H2 downturn in some regions, such as Morocco, Italy, Germany and North America. In its industry segment, sales fell by 1.3% y-o-y. The segment saw a major fall in demand from the automotive sector in the second half, with demand for electronic cables from telecoms manufacturers also declining. However, the shipbuilding, railways, aeronautics, and oil and gas sectors remained strong. Nexans saw construction sales fall 4.9% in 2008, but managed to maintain profitability. Sales were particularly hard hit in Europe, falling 11% in 2008. The downturn was particularly marked in the second half as property markets collapsed in many countries. Data: CRU|y|||||||||||| © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 5 of 12 March 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # North America ### **Latest data shows 2008 as even weaker than previously thought** We have updated our preliminary numbers for 2008 and these now show that North American consumption of copper wire and cable products was at 1,874,000 tonnes conductor in 2008, a decline of 11.8% vs. 2007. As a result of the continuing weakness especially in the automotive, construction and appliances sectors, all the three wire and cable segments showed a y-o-y decline, with winding wire showing the largest decline from prior year at 16.5%, and the energy cable segment showing a 12.4% y-oy decline. The communication cable segment was down by 4.7% from the prior year. North American wirerod consumption declined by 11.5% from the prior year, with Mexico registering the highest fall of 12.9%. North American consumption dropped by 25% in Q4 08 to 384,000 tonnes conductor from 512,000 tonnes conductor recorded in Q3 08. This can be attributed to the aggressive sentiment prevailing amongst manufacturers to reduce inventory due to factors such as the sharp drop in copper prices, the continued economic slowdown, and efforts to maintain cash flow ahead of the year-end. Copper wirerod production declined by 10.2% in 2008 vs. 2007, with Mexico registering the largest fall of 15.8%. Copper wirerod demand dropped by 1.3% more than production due to lower rod imports from Brazil and Russia. ### **Construction sector still under pressure** According to the US Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development, new housing units autho

rized by building permits declined by 4.8% from 547,000 in December 2008 to 521,000 in January 2009. This was 50% down on January 2008. New housing starts declined by 16.8% in January 2009 to 466,000, compared to 560,000 recorded in December 2008. As a result of the still weakening residential construction market, demand for residential building wire is expected to continue to fall in Q1 2009. In terms of commercial building wire, demand has been relatively flat since 3Q 08 but is expected to decline in 2009. Though some observers believe that US government spending on the construction sector will bolster demand later in 2009, it is unlikely to lead to any positive return from the industry in the near future. Moreover, new-build projects that are currently in progress will be completed and very few new-build projects are expected to commence this year. ### **Is there a chance of recovery?** According to industry sources, the market in Q1 09 is holding at equivalent levels to Q4 08. Since Q1 08 was reasonably strong, sources predict a y-o-y drop of 10-15% in Q1 09, with a further fall of maybe 5- 10% in Q2 09, in comparison to Q2 08. The North American automotive sector has seen a significant decline in terms of production due to the weakening global demand and reduced availability of funds. It is predicted that 2009 will see the lowest level of automotive production in America since 1982 and this will inevitably impact on demand for automotive wire and also winding wire. The outlook for the North American market remains unpredictable at this moment across the whole region, but it is possible to still find some people who believe that the second half of this year could see the first signs of a recovery. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 7 of 12 March 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** # North East Asia ### **Japanese cable industry will slip into the red in this financial year** Japanese copper wire and cable shipments fell by 17.7% year-on-year in December to just 57,600 tonnes conductor. Most sectors saw a fall, with the only one showing some growth being communication cables. The automotive sector has been particularly badly hit with automotive wire shipments down by 31.4%. The slump in this sector is also impacting on demand for winding wire. In January shipments fell by 21.2% to 53,100 tonnes, with only the electric power sector reporting any growth, and the automotive sector down by almost 40%. In the face of declining demand and falling profitability most companies are looking at ways of cutting costs and Furukawa is to consolidate its production of copper wires by closing its operations at Chiba and concentrating production at Mie. The Chiba facility will continue to make communication cables. SWCC Showa has reported revenue for the period Q2-Q4 2008 of ¥148.7bn, which is 7.5% lower than in the same period in 2007, with a small operating loss. In the same period Mitsubishi Cable Industries has reported sales of ¥73.6bn, down 6.2%, with an operating loss of 2.7% of sales. One cable company that has reported a profit for Q2-Q4 2008 i

s Furukawa Electric with sales of ¥844bn, just 2.6% down year-onyear, with an operating margin of 3.0%. However, for the full financial year ending March 2009, the company only expects to break even at an operating level and to record a net loss of ¥29bn. In response to the deterioration in the cable sector Sumitomo Electric has said that salaries for managers will be cut by 5% and for executives by 7-20% for the period February to December this year. ### **Taiwanese manufacturers see sales slump in January** Full year 2008 data for Taiwan is now in and this shows that winding wire production fell by 16.5% by volume, whilst electronic wire production fell by 13.0%. The winding wire sector was hit by falling demand for exports, as the Chinese market slowed, and local consumption fell as exports of goods containing winding wire fell. Similarly the electronic wire sector has been hit by a drop in demand for electronic equipment. Demand for cables for use in infrastructure, such as power and telecom cable, was not so badly affected, with production in these sectors down by 5.7% and 2.4% respectively. The fall in production of wire and cable saw sales at Walsin Lihwa, Taiwan’s largest cable manufacturer, drop by 8.6% in 2008 to NT$72.8bn, with sales at Pacific Electric, the second largest cable producer, falling by 4.0% to NT$20.7bn. Leading winding wire manufacturer Jung Shing Wire, recorded a drop of almost 20% in sales value in 2008. As we move into the new year cable companies are having to cope with not only a continuing weakening of the market, but also much lower copper prices, and the impact of this can be seen in January’s company results. Jung Shing Wire has reported sales of NT$124m, compared to sales of NT$593m in January 2008. This is a fall of almost 80%. Pacific Electric Wire and Cable had sales of just NT$555m, a fall of almost 75% from NT$2170m in January 2008, whilst Walsin Lihwa’s sales were NT$2673m, less than half the NT$5936 reported in the previous year. Ta Ya Electric’s sales fell by 66% to NT$331m and of the leading Taiwanese cable manufacturers only HoldKey Electric saw sales drop by less than 50%. Clearly with turnover falling sharply profitability is being severely impacted, and this may be the catalyst for a long awaited industry consolidation. © 2009 CRU International Ltd **confidential** Page 8 of 12 March 2009 Copper wire, cable and wirerod **www.crugroup.com** |North East A|sian copp|er w|ire &

GDP growth in the fourth quarter of 2008 was 6.8%, and the bank acknowledges that the country faces potential deflation and further pressures on economic growth. However, it points to the US$586bn economic stimulus package announced in November plus other initiatives to help the automobile and real estate sectors which will support economic growth this year. To support the real estate sector the government is looking at a range of initiatives such as scrapping curbs

on second homes, cutting taxes for buying and selling property and helping low income people to buy homes. There are also reports that the government could buy some housing stock to help stabilise the market. 

The economic crisis that has hit the global economy has led to reduced demand for a range of goods manufactured in China and destined for export, and this has hit demand for wire and cable used in these products such as winding wire and appliance wire. The stimulus packages are mainly aimed at infrastructure projects and so are most likely to impact on demand for wire and cable used in this sector such as building wire and power cable. Thus the balance of the cable market is set to shift this year. For example the State Grid Corporation of China (SGCC) is planning to more than double its investment for the next two years to US$170bn, to be used for new grid construction and upgrading in urban areas in central and western parts of the country and also in rural areas. Whilst much of this will take the form of overhead lines which use aluminium conductors, some cable in urban areas will need to be installed underground and will use copper conductors, plus there will be a need for winding wire for use in associated transformers. It’s still too early to say if the measures that the government are taking will be successful, and the world will be watching how the Chinese market develops this year, since it is the single most important factor that will determine how the global market turns out in 2009. 

### **Could 2009 see an opening of the Iranian market?** 

With a large population and vast reserves of oil and gas Iran has long been seen as a potentially large market for wire and cable, but its political isolation has meant that this potential has yet to be realised. The Iranian cable industry remains very fragmented with a large number of small locally owned often generalist manufacturers producing relatively low technology cable in old factories which, like much of the rest of the country, have been starved of outside investment. There are though signs that 2009 could mark a turning point for the fortunes of the Iranian cable market. The change of government in the US could lead to a thawing of relations between the two countries, and the decision of the reformist candidate Mohammad Khatami to stand in the June presidential election against Mahmoud Ahmadinejad could result in a shift in economic policy. Already the government is considering relaxing rules on foreign investment, by raising the limit of foreign ownership from 10% to 25%, and also scrapping a rule locking in investment for three years. Of course the big question of Iran’s nuclear ambitions remains to be satisfactorily resolved, but if this can be done then this year may turn out to be the one where the Iranian market finally starts to realise its undoubted potential.

# Industry News 

**Fujian Nanping Sun Cable Co. Ltd** (Nanping Cable) is planning to build a 100k tpy copper rod project. The total investment will be Yuan180m. The first stage is to construct a 30k tpy line, due to start operation in September this year. The second stage will expand this to 100k tpy capacity. 

**East African Cables** has recently commissioned a new copper cable production line at its new Nairobi facility, and is planning further upgrades which when complete will boost production capacity by 60%. The company is keen to increase export sales to other African countries. 

**Nexans** is to close its power transmission cable plant at Quebec in Canada, as part of a reorganisation of its North American operations. 

A number of antitrust authorities around the world have begun investigations into the HV land cable and subsea power cable sectors. Both **Prysmian** and **Nexans** have announced that EU investigators have visited their offices, and authorities in Japan, South Korea and the US are also reported to be conducting their own investigations. In Japan **J-Power** , **Viscas** and **Exsym** are under investigation. 

**Sumitomo Electric Wintec** will cease production of winding wire at its US plant in fiscal 2009. This is as a result of a decline in automobile-related demand in the US and a shift of shipments for consumer electronics to Asia. 

**Fujikura** is planning to relocate production of automotive harnesses from its four plants in Romania to Morocco, to reduce costs and be closer to its main customers in Spain.
